title: Feedback cooling of a levitated nanoparticle in a radially polarized vector beam trap
authors: Felipe Almeida, M. Rademacher, J. M. H. Gosling, P. F. Barker
abstract: We demonstrate optical levitation and feedback cooling of a silica nanoparticle (radius = 78~nm) trapped within a radial vector beam (RVB) in high vacuum. Radial vector beams, when focused by a high-NA lens, produce a smaller focal spot than conventional Gaussian beams, yielding tighter optical potentials and potentially reduced photon-recoil heating rates. A vortex wave plate was used to generate the RVB using an aspheric lens (NA = 0.77) to form the trap. Cold-damping feedback was used to cool the center of mass motion in the radial and axial trap directions to temperatures in the mK range. At higher temperatures and pressures, additional trap frequencies arising from the nonlinear RVB optical potential are observed. This demonstration is a step toward exploiting structured light for levitated quantum optomechanics where these traps can be used to suppress bulk and motional heating.
summary: The authors demonstrated optical levitation and feedback cooling of a nanoparticle trapped by a radially polarized vector beam (RVB). By utilizing RVBs, they created tighter optical potentials than conventional traps, achieving cooling temperatures in the millikelvin range. This work advances the use of structured light for high-precision levitated quantum optomechanics experiments.
main_problem: To develop optical traps that overcome the heating limitations of conventional Gaussian beam traps for use in levitated quantum optomechanics.
main_result: The experiment successfully demonstrated feedback cooling of a nanoparticle trapped in a radially polarized vector beam (RVB) to the mK temperature range.
method: Cold-damping feedback was applied using FPGA control based on measured particle displacement to cool the center-of-mass motion in radial and axial directions.
model_or_system: The system involves a silica nanoparticle levitated in a high vacuum, trapped by a radially polarized vector beam (RVB) generated using a vortex wave plate and aspheric lens.
key_observables: Center-of-mass temperatures ($T_{CM,X}, T_{CM,Z}$), trap frequencies ($\Omega_z, \Omega_x$), and the Power Spectrum Density (PSD) of the particle motion.

paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, the generation and characterization of the RVB trap, the implementation of cold-damping feedback, and the measurement of cooling performance and nonlinear dynamics.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the experimental realization of quantum control in mechanical oscillators by using structured light, which is a key area bridging quantum optics and cavity QED.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: A schematic diagram of the experimental setup used to levitate nanoparticles in the radially polarized beam trap. The radial beam is created by a vortex plate (VP) and is characterized by a polarizer and a CCD (mode monitor) when the flip mirror is raised. After characterization, the radial beam is sent to an aspherical lens with high numerical aperture (NA = 0.77) to form the optical trap. The scattered light from the nanopar- ticle is collected by a collector lens (NA = 0.55). A bal- anced detection scheme is used to measure displacement of the nanoparticle and to cool the center of mass mo- tion along the transverse x and axial z trap axes. A third channel (ROT DET) is also used...

FIG. 2: Polarization characterization of the radially po- larized beam. The radial beam is filtered by rotating a polarizer from 0,45 , 90 and 135 degrees when positioned in front of the CCD camera. It generates four polariza- tion states a) IH, b) I+45, c) IV and d) I−45. The Stokes vectors e) S1 = IH −IV and f) S2 = I+45 −I−45 are computed and the reconstructed polarization map of the radial beam is shown in g).

FIG. 4: Recorded power spectral densities under feed- back cooling for a levitated particle with nominal radius R = 78 nm at three different pressures. Motion is cooled to the noise floor level. The nonlinear peak denoted by X1 dominates the spectra at P = 3.9 × 10−6 mbar.

FIG. 3: a) Transverse intensity for different filling factor 1/β0. Low filling factors prevent formation of a central intensity maximum. b) Transverse intensity profile for 1/β0 = 2.5 assumed in the simulations.
